However, there is overwhelming evidence that the candidate heavily used AI to complete the assessment, and the instructions have been recently updated to explicitly forbid the use of AI. It is impossible for me to be completely certain the candidate used AI, but I will include some supporting evidence: 1) The Excel workbook is full of patterns that AI tools tend to implement, such as using italicized footnotes in a different font size and color to provide context, using multicolored rows to distinguish tables, heavily labeling all data with resized row widths, applying lots of conditional formatting beyond what is necessary, etc. As someone who now regularly uses Claude as a plug-in in Excel, these are all familiar patterns. 2) This one is harder to put a finger on, but the written language is also structured how AI models tend to write for these sorts of assignments, like providing unnatural amounts of detail in some places ("Illinois/Wisconsin (Chicago, Milwaukee, Madison, Gary)"), overly-citing statistics, and making callouts way outside of the scope of this assessment without citing any sources, such as referencing Sprint's "2.5 GHz spectrum" being weaker indoors and referencing that "T-Mobile's 'Un-carrier' offers were aggressive in 2014." The way the workbook data is physically linked to the answer sheet (beyond just simple = formulas) also seems somewhat unlikely human behavior to me. Prior to the instructions being updated I would likely have passed this candidate through, but now that the instructions specifically forbid AI use (and considering how overwhelming the evidence is that they used AI), I'm recommending not passing them through. If this candidate is moved to the next round, checking their Excel skills should be a top priority
